chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
title: Birth, arrival in New Orleans 1904, first blues and Kennedy's My Honey Baby
summary: Carew gives his family origins and moves to New Orleans, recalling the 1904 Labor Day parade, blues fragments in Gretna, and Kennedy's arranged blues My Honey Baby.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: musical inclinations. Well, it's a long time ago. I was born in Michigan, Grand Rapids, and on December the 15th, 1883, and now in my 78th year, my folks came to Michigan from Canada. My father's father, having emigrated from Somersetshire in England to Nova Scotia, then traveled west to Ontario, and my father and the remainder of the family moved over into Michigan in the 1880. I grew up in Grand Rapids when I was 17, and in my 18th year, really, I went to New York for a season, got a job, and earned my living for a while. Went back to Grand Rapids, stayed until 1904, and went down on the Gulf Coast to visit my grandparents, who were living in Mississippi City at that time, my mother's father and mother. And I stayed there until September 1904, when I went into New Orleans. I went to work for the New Orleans Acid and Fertilizer Company, which was a branch of the Union Oil Company. The plant was in Gretna, Louisiana, and I worked at the plant for a couple of years. I went to work in New Orleans on Labor Day of 1904. I went down to the city office, which was in the Hibernia Bank and Trust Building, and waited in the office on the eighth floor, I believe it was, for the superintendent to come from Gretna, where the factory was located, and pick me up and take me over to my new job. I came, while we were waiting there, there was a sudden burst of music from Carondelet Street, right below the windows of the Hibernia Bank and Trust Company, and everybody went to the windows and looked out. Happened to be the Negro Labor Day Parade, 1904. That was my first introduction to New Orleans music, and I must say that it struck me as being very lively, good marching music. They were stepping along in fine shape down Carondelet Street. There were several bands in the parade, but I don't recollect much about them. But in as much as the year was 1904, and they've talked so much about Buddy Bolden being on the scene then, I feel that possibly he was one of the players, and his band must have been in the parade. And then I went over, the superintendent came along and carried me over to Gretna, which is on the other side of the river, opposite Jackson Avenue, New Orleans. While in Gretna, I got my first introduction to what you might call little blues tunes, speaking of characteristic music. They weren't good and they weren't complete, but the office boy, who was a white boy by the way, about 13 years old, must have heard his older brothers singing these little rye-balled strains. And well, they weren't all rye-balled, but some of them were rather rye-balled. And one of the first ones turned out later to go into the song, which was the Hesitation Blues. Hello, Central, what's the matter with this line? I want to talk to that high brown of mine. Tell me how long must I wait? Do I get you now or do I hesitate? Well, he sang that and a couple others maybe on that order. And he also had a fragment of what Jelly Roll wrote up later as Buddy Bolden's Blues. He sang it about Miss Susie. Thought I heard Miss Susie shout. Open up the window and let the breeze blow out. And he had any number of them. One that would go with Hesitation Blues was, I was born in the country, raised in town. I'm a backbone breaker from my navel down. Tell me how. I have to wait. Well, he sang. As I say, he must have gotten them from his older brothers. They were a hot bunch around there. But right across from the fertilizer office over there was the Chickasaw Cooperage office. And the bookkeeper over there was a very fine gentleman by the name of R. Emmett Kennedy. He was of a very old family around that side of the river there. Harvey, I believe, the family lived. And he was bookkeeper of the Chickasaw Cooperage Company. He was a bachelor. And he had a little, he rented a little, a little house, small house opposite the Cooperage Company. And he lived there alone. Well, he had one Negro servant, I believe. He was a musician. He had a grand piano in the place. And it was his hobby to get the Negroes in there in the Coopert Company. Any of them that knew any music, anything of that sort, come over there. And he would pick up their tunes and play them on the piano. And he arranged a couple of books of what he called mellows, which were their tunes. And he arranged the first complete blues. It wasn't maybe much of a real blues, but it was a blues tune called My Honey Baby. And that was afterwards published in a book called Mellows that he published.
The music as well as the words?

The music and words. And this was about 1904 and 1905 that I heard, heard him play that. And I had heard my, I heard the office boy that, that sang these fragments of blues. I'd heard him sing little parts of that. Oh, my honey baby, she can cook and stew. She's a good doing baby through and through, but she's got low down ways. And something of that sort, you know. But just little fragments that this office boy sang. But anyhow, in 1906, Kennedy gave a concert in Algiers. And he played the piano and his niece sang the songs. Of course, he played some instrumental music also. But he had several songs that she sang, and she sang this Honey Baby at that time. Honey Baby. And that, that was the first blues I ever heard. And it was, as I say, I heard it in 1906 when he had arranged it. Well, the question came up later about the early date on blues. And I wrote to Kennedy, who had gone to New York and was in New York, and asked him when, when he arranged that tune. And he said, well, he had arranged it several years before the concert that I mentioned in Algiers. So that would place it at least about 1903, which was an early date. Well, what is the title of it? My Honey Baby. Honey Baby. I don't think there's Ma there.
Honey Baby. As you remember, it was the familiar blues chords.

It had blues chords in it, blues notes in it. But it didn't stick strictly to the 12 bars. You might have, you might have called it a 14 bar maybe, or you, but it didn't stand strictly with that, the 12 bar as the, as it was afterwards the, the Orthodox real country blues was a 12 bar thing that they, that they held it to. But it did have the blue notes in it. And I asked him, I wrote Kennedy and asked him, he was in New York at the time, I wrote and asked him when he had arranged it. He said it was several years before he gave that concert. He had done it. He, he did it with the help of the man servant that worked for him, Negro man. But he afterwards published it.
